Body: This happens to me too. I'm using ubuntu with the kitty terminal.

Supplement:
- This issue does not duplicate any existing issues.
- I suspect there may be a conflict between the opencode beta sub-agent message transmission mechanism and the latest version of opencode. I just rolled back the WSL opencode version from v1.17.8 to v1.17.0, and the opencode beta client can successfully launch sub-agents after connecting to WSL.
- I'm not sure whether I should raise this issue on the opencode repository, but the opencode beta repository cannot accept issues. Sorry for the disturbance.

Clarification: this appears to be a workspace-level billing bug, not just a duplicate invoice.

From what I remember, I first subscribed to OpenCode Go, but the dashboard did not show an active/manageable subscription. Because of that, I tried subscribing again through other workspace/account states. It seems one email/account can have multiple workspaces, and each workspace can have its own Go subscription.

This likely created multiple Go subscriptions under the same email/payment method. The visible workspace subscriptions were later cancelled / payment method removed, but at least one earlier subscription appears to have become orphaned or hidden and kept charging.

So the core issue is that a Go subscription can exist at the workspace/billing level while not being visible or manageable from the user’s current dashboard/account view.

Please audit all workspace, customer, and subscription records linked to my email/GitHub account/payment method, not only the currently visible workspace.

Could you please reopen this PR? 🙏

It was closed automatically by the bot due to age, but **it fixes a real and reproducible bug that was previously reported that you wanted to be fixed since the last year**: #28538, where the TUI loses interactivity and prints ANSI noise when stdin is piped. This also matches the older related reports #24195, #3871, and #6220.

@thdxr Updated shape: `--yolo` is now the canonical option; `--dangerously-skip-permissions` is retained only as a legacy alias.

### Examples

```sh
# TUI
opencode --yolo

# Non-interactive run
opencode run --yolo "refactor the auth module"

# Headless server
OPENCODE_YOLO=1 opencode serve

# Legacy forms remain compatible
opencode --dangerously-skip-permissions
OPENCODE_DANGEROUSLY_SKIP_PERMISSIONS=1 opencode serve
```

Both CLI spellings normalize to `yolo`, and both environment variables feed the same server-side runtime flag. The permission service auto-approves `ask` decisions while still enforcing explicit `deny` rules. An already-running remote server must have been started with `OPENCODE_YOLO=1`; `attach` cannot change that server process.

There've been a few takes on this already (#24210 most recently) that got auto-closed without ever being reviewed. Before I redo that work, is this something you'd actually accept, and is there a shape you want?

I went digging through the code first and a decent chunk already exists: `GET /api/session/:sessionID/context` gives you the messages after the last compaction, and every assistant message already stores the provider's real token counts (input/output/cache). So the accurate total and the % used are basically free.

The part that has to be estimated is the per-category split: system, tools, chat history, tool results, file reads. I'd estimate those roughly (chars/4) and then get the system+tools overhead by subtracting the estimated history from the real input total the provider already reported. That way the overhead number stays grounded and I don't have to rebuild the whole system prompt to measure it.

Shape I had in mind: compute it in core (new `context-usage.ts`), put it on a sibling endpoint, TUI dialog on `/context` plus a leader keybind, and the desktop sidebar can reuse the same endpoint later.

One thing I'd want your call on: is an estimate (chars/4) fine for v1, or do you want a real tokenizer? I'd rather not pull tiktoken in just for this.

Happy to put up a small PR if the shape sounds right.

the duplicate-pickup problem @ThinkOffApp and @m13v hit (two agents grabbing the same task off an append-only room) is the bit that turns "multi-agent" into a real coordination problem rather than just spawning processes.

for what its worth i went after this from outside the CLI with [repowire](https://github.com/prassanna-ravishankar/repowire), a cross-runtime mesh: each session gets a mesh address and they ask/ack/notify/broadcast over a local daemon, with spawn/kill for the conductor pattern. the claim/mutex issue is handled by the job + schedule primitives rather than polling a shared file.

the angle that might be useful here: because its runtime-neutral, the "team" can be mixed (an opencode conductor driving a claude or codex worker), which matters when one model is better at a given lane. not native opencode, but its a working version of the conductor+isolated-workers shape today.

the modal/blocking delegation is the core thing, agreed. the parent shouldnt have to stop and babysit a child to completion.

one external pattern that gives you this today: [repowire](https://github.com/prassanna-ravishankar/repowire) (a cross-runtime agent mesh). a peer fires `ask` or `notify` to another peer and carries on, the child runs in its own session, and the result comes back as a deferred ack rather than blocking the caller. un-acked asks resurface on the next turn so nothing gets silently dropped.

honest framing: repowire peers are separate sessions on a daemon, not in-process background subagents, so its not the exact native shape youre asking opencode for. but if youre blocked on fire-and-forget delegation right now its a way to get it, and it works across runtimes too.

the named-messaging-between-flat-teams shape in this design is the right call, and a couple of things from having shipped roughly this externally that might be worth baking in:

- address by stable identity, not display name. spawned same-path agents collide on name, so routing has to canonicalise to an id underneath or you get intermittent misroutes
- give asks a correlation id and an explicit ack, so a sender can tell delivered vs queued vs blocked. fire-and-forget hides the failure case that actually bites

i built [repowire](https://github.com/prassanna-ravishankar/repowire) as the cross-runtime version of this (ask/ack/notify/broadcast over a local daemon, peer_id identity). not opencode-native, but if its useful as a reference for the messaging/identity layer the design is open. the TUI-integration piece @FurryWolfX wants is the part an external mesh cant give you, so native is genuinely better there.

the no-public-server constraint is the important one here, thats what makes most "remote control" setups a pain to trust.

[repowire](https://github.com/prassanna-ravishankar/repowire) does this shape today: the daemon stays local and a hosted relay bridges to it, so you steer and answer permission/question prompts from your phone (telegram/slack) without exposing a port. inbound messages route to the session and the reply comes back the same way.

honest gap vs what youre asking: repowire goes through chat apps rather than a first-party QR-paired web view, so its not the polished native pairing flow. but the run-local, steer-from-phone, no-public-server part works now if you need it before a first-party version exists.

this is the exact problem i ended up solving in [repowire](https://github.com/prassanna-ravishankar/repowire), and the `heartbeat_at` + `peer_id` shape you propose is almost the same design i landed on, so a couple of notes from running it:

- keying on a stable `peer_id` rather than a path/name is the right call. parallel sessions on the same project collide on anything path-derived, so liveness and routing both need the id
- on the heartbeat: i deliberately avoided a polling timer. instead liveness is reconciled lazily, when a request next needs the registry it runs a repair pass and evicts stale peers. nothing runs on a schedule, the work piggybacks on real requests. cheaper, and no background loop to babysit

the crashed-session-leaks-resources case is real and ghost eviction handles it well once you have the id + a reconciliation trigger. happy to share specifics if useful, this is squarely the thing the daemon does.

the persistent-daemon-alongside-the-main-agent model with push and pull is basically the architecture [repowire](https://github.com/prassanna-ravishankar/repowire) is built on, so a data point on whether it holds up: it does, and the push/pull split is the right framing.

how it shakes out in practice: pull is the agent asking the daemon for something (ask), push is the daemon delivering an event into the session unprompted (notify). the one design decision that mattered most was keeping the daemon the only hub and making how a session connects (hook, socket, bot) a client concern, so routing and lifecycle dont have to learn about each transport.

its cross-runtime and external rather than native to opencode, but the persistent-daemon-with-bidirectional-coordination shape youre sketching is proven out if its useful as prior art.

the bot-must-spawn-its-own-server coupling is worth fixing, and theres a more general version of the point: the slack bot is really just one transport into a server, so it shouldnt care where the server runs.

thats the line i drew in [repowire](https://github.com/prassanna-ravishankar/repowire), where the daemon is the only hub and every transport (hooks, bots, relay) is a client that connects to it. so the slack peer can point at a daemon on the same box, another box, or through a relay, and the bot/server colocation problem just doesnt come up. an `OPENCODE_SERVER_URL` env var is exactly the right minimal version of that for the existing bot.
